title: Bitcoin ETF inflows fuelled September's rebound, but the momentum has faded
body: A widely shared post over the weekend claimed BlackRock had bought around $1.6 billion of Bitcoin "this month," citing on-chain data from Arkham. The figure actually covers the past month, so mostly September. It reflects investors buying BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), not BlackRock buying for its own account. The stronger story is how closely those flows tracked Bitcoin's recovery, and what the late-month slowdown might mean. What the BlackRock number really measures IBIT is a spot Bitcoin ETF. When investors buy more of its shares than they sell, new shares are created and the fund buys Bitcoin to back them, which is held by a custodian. When investors sell more than they buy, shares are redeemed and Bitcoin leaves the fund. Arkham tracks the custody wallets where that Bitcoin is held. That makes the figure a measure of client demand through one product. It shows money arrived. It does not show who the buyers were, how long they intend to hold, or whether some are hedged elsewhere. September's flows came in waves The month was far from a steady climb. On September 1, US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $236.5 million, and IBIT accounted for $201 million of that. Two days later the picture flipped: IBIT took in about $454 million on September 3, roughly 62% of all US spot Bitcoin ETF inflows that day. The middle of the month was weak.

title: ANZ commodity index rises 0.6% in September as oil surge lifts milk powder and aluminium
body: Oil is the main channel here. The surge in energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict lifted milk powder and aluminium, the main drivers of September's gains. Combined with a weaker New Zealand dollar, that gives exporters a solid boost in local-currency returns, which supports farm incomes and the terms of trade. The flip side is higher import and freight costs, which add to domestic inflation pressure. That could complicate the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's task. If US rates keep pressuring the kiwi lower, the local-currency boost to export earnings is likely to persist. Any easing in oil prices, however, could quickly reverse milk powder's run. ---- Oil is doing New Zealand's dairy farmers a favour and a weak kiwi is doubling it, though the same conflict is pushing up the freight bill. Summary: The ANZ World Commodity Price Index rose 0.6% m/m in September and is up 1.0% y/y, with gains in most categories. The rise was largely driven by sharply higher oil and gas prices. Skim milk powder jumped 9.2% m/m and is up 41.1% y/y. Butter fell 5.1%. Aluminium rose 1.1% on Middle East supply disruption. Freight costs also rose. The NZD index rose 2.8% as the New Zealand dollar weakened, partly on higher US interest rates. New Zealand's export commodity prices rose in September, ANZ Research said. The increase was lifted largely by a sharp rise in oil and gas prices tied to the Middle East conflict, while a weaker New Zealand dollar magnified the gains for local exporters.

title: BOJ's Uchida says AI is a big demand shock lifting prices, warns of correction risk
body: Uchida describes AI as an inflationary demand shock that has loosened financial conditions, which leans hawkish. It argues that the BOJ's tightening has more to do, without signalling a timetable. That supports the yen at the margin and keeps further BOJ hike expectations intact. His point that AI-related bond supply is pushing up long-term yields adds a new, non-monetary explanation for the pressure on global bond markets, including JGBs. The warning about a correction if profits don't follow is a reminder that the central bank is watching equity valuations, so any AI-led selloff could feed straight into its assessment of financial conditions. --- The BOJ sees AI as a demand boom first and a productivity story later, which means more inflation now and a correction risk if the profits never arrive. Summary: BOJ Deputy Governor Uchida said AI has been a big positive demand shock, putting upward pressure on the economy and prices. He said AI is a key topic at BOJ policy meetings, with implications for the output gap, financial conditions and star variables such as the neutral rate. AI has boosted stocks and eased financial conditions, while heavy AI-related bond issuance has pushed up long-term rates. His tentative view is that demand effects came first, leaving conditions more accommodative on balance, with a correction risk if profits don't follow. Longer term, AI could lift productivity and capital stock, with mixed effects on labour markets.

title: Gold Rises as Fed Rate Hike Bets Ease
body: Gold rose above $4,150 an ounce on Monday, retracing part of the previous session's losses after weaker-than-expected US employment data eased pressure on the Federal Reserve to continue raising interest rates. Figures released on Friday showed the US economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, far below the consensus forecast of a 90,000 increase, following a downwardly revised gain of 133,000 in August. The unemployment rate climbed to 4.2%, while annual wage growth unexpectedly slowed to 3.0%, its weakest pace since May 2021. Following the data, markets moved to price in nearly an 80% probability that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its meeting this month, while expectations for a December hike held around 69%. At the same time, persistently elevated US Treasury yields continued to pressure precious metals, with the 10-year yield trading near its highest level since 2002. Investor sentiment was further influenced by mounting geopolitical risks in the Middle East, as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched a full-scale military offensive to retake territory held by Iran-aligned Houthi fighters. title: Japan Private Sector Growth Revised Slightly Lower

Although this marked the 18th consecutive month of private-sector expansion, it was the slowest pace of growth since May, with activity moderating in both manufacturing and services. Total new business rose at a gentler and more moderate rate, while new export orders remained robust, driven entirely by the manufacturing sector. Employment increased at its fastest pace since February, accompanied by a stronger rise in backlogs of work, pointing to persistent capacity pressures. On the pricing front, inflationary pressures stayed historically elevated, though the rates of increase in both input costs and output charges eased compared with August. Finally, business confidence climbed to a seven-month high, indicating that firms remain optimistic about activity over the year ahead. title: Singapore Private Sector Growth Remains Strong
body: Singapore's S&P Global PMI eased to 58.1 in September 2026 from a record 59.4 in August, but continued to indicate a strong improvement in private‑sector business conditions. Growth was underpinned by a marked increase in new orders, supported by robust demand, an expanding customer base, and successful business development efforts, all of which helped to accelerate overall activity. Real estate and business services posted the sharpest gains in both new orders and output. Rising workloads led firms to step up hiring and purchasing and to build inventories. However, supplier performance worsened significantly, with lead times lengthening at their fastest pace since early 2022. Cost pressures also intensified: input price inflation rose to a survey peak, prompting companies to lift output prices at one of the quickest rates on record. Despite these headwinds, business confidence stayed positive, underpinned by expectations of better market conditions, new product launches, and supportive government initiatives. title: Japanese Shares Climb on Soft US Jobs Data
body: The Nikkei 225 Index surged more than 2% toward the 70,000 level on Monday, hitting a three-month high after weaker-than-expected US employment data eased pressure on the Federal Reserve to pursue further interest rate hikes. Nonetheless, sentiment remained cautious as bond yields stayed elevated and geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East persisted. On the domestic front, investors are awaiting a slate of key economic indicators due this week, including figures on wage growth, household spending, and consumer confidence. In corporate developments, SoftBank Group Corp. founder Masayoshi Son—one of the most prominent advocates for artificial intelligence—said he is increasingly worried about safety risks as machines rapidly gain new capabilities. He called on governments worldwide to foster trust and cooperate more closely to harness AI responsibly. Technology and AI-related stocks led the advance, with notable gains in Kioxia Holdings (up 1.3%), Advantest (4.4%), SoftBank Group (3.3%), Tokyo Electron (3.2%), and Taiyo Yuden (3%). title: Australian Shares Rise Further as Week Begins
body: Australian shares climbed 32 points, or 0.4%, to 8,714 in early Monday trade, extending gains for a second session as most sectors advanced. Industrial services, consumer durables, and financials led the market higher, supported by firmer U.S. equity futures after softer jobs data reduced pressure on the Federal Reserve to deliver another rate hike. Domestically, September private-sector growth was revised higher, driven by strength in services, even as manufacturing output remained subdued. Trading volumes were partly constrained by holiday-thinned activity in several states, including New South Wales and Queensland, while markets in key trading partner China stayed shut for the Golden Week holiday. Treasurer Jim Chalmers noted that the conflict in the Middle East is now a key driver of Australia's inflation challenge, maintaining pressure on the Reserve Bank to preserve a hawkish stance. Among major stocks, the big four banks rose between 0.4% and 0.9%, while BHP and Rio Tinto each gained close to 1%. Other notable performers included Reece, up 1.6%, and Codan, up 1.9%. In contrast, QBE Insurance fell 1.7% and Lynas Rare Earths slipped 1%. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Irish Services Growth Slows to 4-Month Low
body: The AIB Ireland Services PMI eased to 54.1 in September 2026, down from August's eight-month high of 55.4, and reached its lowest level since May. This signalled a moderation in services-sector growth for the first time since April and a move below the long-run average. Despite the softer headline reading, demand strengthened, supported by broad-based expansion across sectors for a second consecutive month. Technology, media and telecommunications recorded the fastest rate of growth. New business rose at its quickest pace in ten months, driven by new client wins and intensified marketing efforts, although growth in new export business was only marginal. Employment continued to edge higher, even as backlogs of work increased further. On the inflation front, input costs rose at their fastest rate since May, largely reflecting higher fuel and energy prices. In turn, firms increased their selling prices at the quickest pace in five months. Business confidence strengthened, reaching its highest level since February 2025, underpinned by planned investment, expectations of new contracts, and ongoing marketing initiatives. title: US Futures Edge Higher as Rate Hike Bets Fade
body: US stock index futures inched higher on Monday, extending last session's gains after softer US employment data eased pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates. Nasdaq 100 futures rose about 0.3%, while futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 added roughly 0.1% each. On Friday, Wall Street advanced after data showed US employers created fewer jobs than expected in September and wage growth slowed. Markets are now assigning nearly an 80% chance that the Fed will leave interest rates unchanged at its upcoming meeting. Even so, traders remained wary of elevated Treasury yields, with the 10-year yield hovering near its highest level since 2002. Investors are looking ahead to a new slate of economic indicators this week for further guidance, including the ISM services index, minutes from the Fed's September meeting and the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey. Corporate earnings are also due from Constellation Brands, Levi Strauss, PepsiCo, Delta Air Lines and other major companies. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Oil Steady as Traders Weigh Middle East Risks
body: Crude oil prices hovered near $91 per barrel on Monday as investors focused on escalating tensions in the Middle East, while OPEC+ opted to keep production quotas unchanged for next month. Saudi-backed forces in Yemen launched a full-scale military offensive to recapture territories held by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement, following weeks of rising friction between the two sides. The Houthis have seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key maritime chokepoint between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden that Saudi Arabia had been using as an alternative export route to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, leading OPEC+ producers agreed over the weekend to maintain current output targets despite ongoing supply disruptions linked to the regional conflict. The decision comes as crude prices move back toward the $100-per-barrel mark and diesel prices hit record highs at the pump, prompting G7 countries to tap emergency oil reserves in response to the continuing turmoil. title: Australia Services Growth Revised Upward
body: The S&P Global Australia Services PMI Business Activity Index slipped to 51.9 in September 2026 from 53.2 in August, though it exceeded the preliminary estimate of 51.4. This marked a fourth consecutive month of expansion, but growth slowed to its weakest pace in three months as new business rose at the softest rate in the current three‑month upturn. Export activity improved, with overseas demand increasing for the first time in five months, albeit only marginally. Employment declined for the first time since May, as firms pointed to weaker new orders and cost‑containment efforts. Meanwhile, backlogs of work continued to rise, extending the current sequence of accumulation to three months. On the price front, input cost inflation accelerated, driven by higher fuel, labour and other operating expenses. Output price inflation also picked up, with firms passing increased costs on to customers. Both input and output price inflation remained above their respective long‑run averages. Business confidence dropped to a three‑month low, with some firms voicing concerns about the broader economic outlook and future sales. title: NZX 50 Trades in the Green to Start the Week
body: The NZX 50 rose 41 points, or 0.3%, to 13,722 in Monday morning trade, reversing losses from the previous two sessions and rebounding from its lowest level since September 15, hit on Friday. The move followed gains on Wall Street after a weaker-than-expected US jobs report tempered expectations of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve. Financials, real estate, and industrials led the broader market higher, while declines in energy, consumer staples, and consumer discretionary stocks limited the overall advance. Investors also looked ahead to this week's release of FOMC meeting minutes and kept a close watch on oil price developments after Yemen's Saudi-backed forces announced a major operation aimed at recapturing all territory held by the Houthis. Early gainers included Port of Tauranga (up 2.5%), Mainfreight (1.2%), Infratil (1.4%), Ebos Group (1.1%), Auckland International Airport (1.0%), FC Investment (1.0%), and Chorus (0.6%). title: Australia Composite PMI Revised Higher
body: Australia's S&P Global Flash Composite PMI for September 2026 was revised up to 51.3 from the preliminary estimate of 50.8, though it remained below August's final reading of 52.7 and was the lowest level since June. Even so, it signaled a fourth consecutive month of expansion in private‑sector activity. The services sector continued to grow, albeit at its slowest pace in three months, while the contraction in manufacturing output intensified amid a renewed decline in new goods orders. Stronger inflows of new business in services kept overall new orders in expansion territory, but total export demand fell, reflecting weaker manufacturing export orders. Employment returned to growth in September. On the price front, output cost inflation quickened. Input and output cost pressures strengthened in the services sector but eased in manufacturing, although they remained high by historical standards. Finally, business confidence deteriorated, slipping to a three‑month low. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com
